questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: NovaLar, an online furniture and home appliance retailer, is building a customer-service resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent accesses the backend through its own MCP tools (get_customer, verify_identity, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), and the goal is to resolve about 70% of tickets without a human. Business constraints: no financial action before the customer's identity is verified, refunds above R$ 2,000 require human approval, and data handling follows the LGPD.

In staging, an audit found 4 cases in 1,000 in which the agent called process_refund before verify_identity, even though the system prompt says in capital letters "ALWAYS verify identity before any refund". What is the MOST appropriate fix?
opcoes: A PreToolUse hook on process_refund that denies the call until there is a successful verify_identity in the session.
Add a second model that reviews each agent response and alerts the team when it detects a refund without prior verification.
Reinforce the system prompt with the rule repeated at the beginning and at the end, plus three few-shot examples of the correct verification-before-refund flow.
Use a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that automatically reverses the refund when it finds no prior identity verification.
questoes.explicacao: Critical rules (financial, security, compliance) belong in deterministic code. PreToolUse intercepts process_refund before execution and denies it with a reason until the verification exists.
feedbacks: Correct. A rule with financial consequences requires deterministic enforcement. The hook blocks the call before it executes and returns the reason, so the model can correct itself (call verify_identity first).
A more complex solution than necessary, and still probabilistic; besides, it detects after the fact, when the refund may already have been issued.
Tempting because it usually lowers the error rate, but a prompt is probabilistic: failures drop, they don't go to zero. Anti-pattern: a critical rule enforced only through the prompt.
Attacks the problem too late: the money has already gone out and the reversal may fail. The place to prevent an action is before it, in PreToolUse.

questoes.pergunta: At NovaLar, the agent loop was hand-written. In some tickets the agent replies "I'll look up your order now" and the conversation ends without any lookup at all. The code ends the loop when the first content block is of type text. What is the fix?
opcoes: Cap the loop at a maximum of 5 iterations and always end on the fifth, ensuring that every tool gets a chance to run.
End the loop only when the text contains a closing phrase such as "Is there anything else I can help you with?", defined in the system prompt.
Instruct the model, in the system prompt, never to write text before calling a tool, so that the first block always indicates the real intent.
Decide by stop_reason: tool_use continues the loop (execute and return tool_result); end_turn ends it.
questoes.explicacao: The agentic loop is driven by stop_reason: tool_use continues, end_turn ends. Having a text block is not a signal that it's finished.
feedbacks: An iteration limit serves as a safety backstop, not as the primary stopping mechanism. It would cut off long tickets and drag out short ones.
Tempting because it looks like an explicit contract, but it is the anti-pattern of deciding termination by reading natural language; the model may vary the phrase.
Treats the symptom through the prompt, with no guarantee. The bug is in the code that ignores stop_reason; text before tool_use is legitimate behavior.
Correct. content can mix text and tool_use in the same response; having text doesn't mean it's finished. What signals continuation or completion is stop_reason.

questoes.pergunta: At NovaLar, the model returned two tool_use blocks in a single response: get_customer and lookup_order. The developer executes both tools and sends two consecutive user messages, each with one tool_result. The next request starts failing. How should the results be returned correctly?
opcoes: Set disable_parallel_tool_use: true so that the model requests one tool at a time and sending them in separate messages works.
A single user message with both tool_result blocks, each with its corresponding tool_use_id.
Return only the get_customer result and discard lookup_order, because the model will request the order again if it needs it.
Send both results concatenated in a single text block of the user message, since the model knows which tools it requested.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple tool_use blocks in one response: execute them (in parallel, if you like) and return all the tool_result blocks in a single user message, each with its tool_use_id.
feedbacks: It works, but trades the fix for a limitation: it loses parallelism and makes the service slower for no reason.
Correct. In parallel tool use, all results go back together in a single user message, each tied to its tool_use_id.
Every tool_use needs a tool_result; leaving one unanswered breaks the conversation and forces repeated calls.
Loses the link to the tool_use_id values; the model and the API expect structured tool_result blocks, not free text.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar requires human approval for refunds above R$ 2,000. Today this exists only in the system prompt and, in testing, the agent sometimes processes R$ 2,350 directly. Which implementation satisfies the rule?
opcoes: Create a PostToolUse hook that, after a process_refund above the limit, automatically opens an audit ticket for a supervisor.
Move the rule to the beginning of the system prompt and add a few-shot example of an R$ 2,500 refund being escalated.
Train a classifier that analyzes each customer message and, when it predicts a high refund, disables the process_refund tool for that turn.
PreToolUse hook on process_refund: above R$ 2,000, it denies the call with a reason that directs the agent to use escalate_to_human.
questoes.explicacao: Financial limit = deterministic enforcement in PreToolUse, with a reason that points toward escalation.
feedbacks: Records the problem after the money has gone out. Auditing is a good complement, but it doesn't prevent the violation.
Improves adherence, but remains probabilistic; with money involved, the failure rate needs to be zero.
Complex, expensive and still probabilistic (the prediction can be wrong). Moreover, changing the tools array between turns invalidates the prompt cache.
Correct. The limit is a financial rule: it belongs in code, before execution. The returned reason helps the agent follow the right path (escalate).

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar's human support staff complain that, with every escalation, they have to reread the entire conversation to understand the case, and they frequently ask the customer for information the customer has already provided. How should the handoff be designed?
opcoes: Ask the model, in free text, to "summarize the conversation for the support rep" before calling escalate_to_human.
Make escalate_to_human require a structured summary (customer, issue, actions taken, reason, recommendation).
Give the support staff access to a dashboard with the raw logs of every tool call made by the agent.
Attach to the ticket the full conversation transcript and the results of every tool called, so that no detail gets lost in the handoff.
questoes.explicacao: A human handoff requires a structured summary: identity, issue, actions taken, reason for the block, recommended action.
feedbacks: Improves things a little, but without defined fields the summary varies and leaves out precisely the IDs, amounts and actions already taken.
Correct. The human usually doesn't see the transcript; a summary with defined fields (validated by the tool's schema) carries the essentials without any rereading.
More raw data to dig through; it doesn't address the need to understand the case quickly.
Tempting because of the completeness argument, but it's exactly what the support staff already do today: reread everything. What's missing is structure, not volume.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar's agent has two tools: lookup_order ("Looks up orders") and get_order_status ("Gets order information"). In 30% of cases it calls the wrong one and needs a second call. What is the first fix to make?
opcoes: Add an intent classifier in front of the agent that decides which of the two tools to enable on each turn.
Configure tool_choice to force lookup_order on every first call and leave get_order_status for subsequent calls.
Include five few-shot examples in the system prompt showing when to use each tool.
Rewrite the descriptions with purpose, when to use, and how each one differs from the other (or merge the two).
questoes.explicacao: A tool description is the selection criterion: purpose, when to use, inputs, outputs, edge cases and how it differs from similar tools.
feedbacks: A more complex solution than necessary. The exam favors fixing the description before creating routing components.
Locks the flow into an external decision tree and fails whenever the case calls for the other tool first.
May help, but treats the symptom; the source of the problem (vague, overlapping descriptions) remains for any case not covered.
Correct. The description is the tool's selection criterion. Overlapping tools with vague descriptions cause misrouting; the simplest fix is to differentiate them (or merge them).

questoes.pergunta: At NovaLar, lookup_order returns {"error": "Operation failed"} both when the orders database times out and when the number doesn't exist. The agent has been telling customers that "the order does not exist" during outages. What is the best redesign?
opcoes: Keep the generic message, but instruct the agent to always retry three times before replying to the customer.
Change the message to "Error looking up order, contact technical support" in both cases.
Separate the cases: "not found" as an empty success; timeout as a structured error (transient, retryable, with the attempted action).
On timeout, return an empty list of orders, so as not to expose technical details to the model.
questoes.explicacao: Structured errors distinguish categories and retryability; a legitimate empty result is not an error.
feedbacks: Blind retries for "not found" waste calls and don't solve anything: the generic message still hides the diagnosis.
Still generic: the model still doesn't know whether to retry, ask for another number or warn about an outage.
Correct. Empty is not failure: "not found" is information. A timeout means the search didn't run, and the structured error allows a retry or an honest answer to the customer.
Silent-suppression anti-pattern: it turns a failure into "nothing found", exactly what caused the problem.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar is classifying process_refund failures so the agent knows how to react. Which TWO failure → handling pairs are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Payment gateway timeout → transient, retryable error: try again with backoff.
Customer account frozen on suspicion of fraud → business error, not retryable: explain the policy or escalate.
Frozen account → transient error: wait a few seconds and try again with exponential backoff.
Refund amount sent as the text "R$ 120.00" instead of a number → escalate immediately to a human.
Expired service token → transient error: repeat the call immediately up to three times.
questoes.explicacao: Transient → retry with backoff; validation → fix the input; business → explain/escalate; permission → escalate.
feedbacks: Correct. Timeouts/unavailability are transient; retry with backoff is the appropriate response.
Correct. A policy limit doesn't change with a new attempt; the agent should explain or escalate.
Confuses business with transient: retrying doesn't unfreeze the account and delays the response to the customer.
It's a validation error: the agent itself fixes the input and tries again; escalating would be wasteful.
A permission error is not retryable: repeating with the same token fails the same way. The path is to escalate/renew the credential.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar added the CRM's remote MCP server to the repository's .mcp.json: {"crm": {"url": "https://mcp.novalar.com/crm"}}. The server doesn't connect, and the log shows an attempt to start a local process. What is the cause?
opcoes: "type": "http" is missing; without type, the entry is treated as stdio.
The SSE transport is mandatory for remote servers; just change the URL so it ends in /sse.
The remote server needs to be in the user scope (~/.claude.json), because .mcp.json only accepts local servers.
The "args" field with the URL is missing, since every MCP server is started as a process with arguments.
questoes.explicacao: In .mcp.json, a remote server requires a declared type ("http"); an entry with url and no type is interpreted as stdio.
feedbacks: Correct. A remote server needs an explicit type (Streamable HTTP, the remote transport with OAuth); without it, it falls back to stdio and fails.
SSE is legacy. The recommended remote transport (and the only remote one with OAuth) is Streamable HTTP.
False: .mcp.json (project scope) accepts remote servers; the scope doesn't explain the attempt to start a local process.
Confuses the transports: command/args is stdio configuration; a remote server uses type/url/headers.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar's system prompt says: "Be reasonable when approving refunds for damaged items". Two nearly identical tickets (sofa with a 5 cm tear, photo attached) receive opposite decisions. Which adjustment resolves the inconsistency?
opcoes: Ask the model to report its confidence (0 to 1) in each decision and automatically reprocess decisions with confidence below 0.8.
Run the decision three times, in independent calls, and adopt the majority vote as the final result.
Replace the vague instruction with explicit criteria: what counts as damage, what doesn't, and borderline examples.
Add "be consistent and fair" to the system prompt.
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria (counts / doesn't count / borderline examples) beat generic instructions like "be reasonable".
feedbacks: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and doesn't define what counts as damage; the criterion remains vague.
Masks the inconsistency at triple the cost; the problem is the lack of criteria, not the sampling.
Correct. "Be reasonable" leaves the judgment up to the model and produces inconsistency; explicit criteria with borderline cases make the decision reproducible.
Yet another vague instruction; it doesn't tell the model what counts and what doesn't.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar's agent confuses "warranty exchange" with "change-of-mind return" in ambiguous tickets (e.g., a customer 40 days after purchase reporting an intermittent defect). Which technique is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Include examples with only input and label, without explanation, so as not to lead the model to copy the reasoning.
Include 30 examples of easy, typical tickets from each category, to cover the largest possible volume.
2 to 4 few-shot examples of varied, ambiguous cases, each with the ticket, classification and reasoning.
Create a separate classification tool that the agent must call before any response.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot: 2–4 targeted, varied examples, with input, output and reasoning, especially for ambiguous cases.
feedbacks: Without the reasoning, the model tends to memorize cases instead of learning the criterion that separates the categories.
Many easy examples don't teach the boundary, which is where the errors are; they also bloat the prompt.
Correct. Few-shot with reasoning, focused on varied edge cases, teaches the decision pattern and generalizes better than prose.
Shifts the problem to another component without teaching the criterion; adds unnecessary complexity.

questoes.pergunta: A NovaLar customer writes in all caps, with profanity, outraged about an improper R$ 15 shipping charge. The policy allows refunding shipping charged in error. What should the agent do?
opcoes: Ask the customer to calm down before continuing with the service.
Acknowledge the frustration, verify the improper charge and resolve the refund within policy, without escalating.
Escalate immediately to a human, because very angry customers should always talk to a person.
Assess its own confidence in the resolution and escalate if it falls below 70%.
questoes.explicacao: Sentiment ≠ complexity: an angry customer with a simple problem covered by policy → resolve it.
feedbacks: Delays the solution to a simple problem and tends to make the experience worse.
Correct. Sentiment is not complexity: the case is simple and covered by policy, so the agent resolves it.
Anti-pattern of escalating based on sentiment. Escalation happens on an explicit request, a policy gap or lack of progress.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and is not an escalation criterion.

questoes.pergunta: At NovaLar, get_customer with the name "Maria Souza" returns three different customers. The customer wants her delivery status. What is the correct behavior for the agent?
opcoes: List the three records with addresses so that the customer can indicate which one is hers.
Ask for an identifier (email, CPF or order no.) to disambiguate.
Choose the record with the most recent order, since it's the most likely.
Escalate to a human, since the search didn't return a single result.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple results for the customer → ask for an identifier to disambiguate; don't guess and don't escalate.
feedbacks: Leaks third parties' personal data. Disambiguation should come from an identifier the customer provides.
Correct. With multiple candidates, the agent asks for an identifier instead of guessing; acting on the wrong customer also violates privacy.
It's a guess. If it's wrong, it exposes another person's data (LGPD) and reports an incorrect status.
Search ambiguity is not a reason for escalation; asking for an identifier is enough.

questoes.pergunta: In long NovaLar conversations, after the history is summarized to fit in the context, the agent has started getting wrong the order number and the agreed refund amount provided at the beginning. Which mitigation is the most appropriate?
opcoes: When in doubt, ask the customer again for the order number and the amount.
Ask, in the summarization prompt, for the model to "preserve important details".
Disable summarization and keep the full conversation history, migrating the agent to a model with a larger context window.
A persistent "case facts" block (IDs, amounts, dates), reinjected on every turn and kept outside the summary.
questoes.explicacao: A case facts block outside the summary preserves exact values that summarization tends to lose.
feedbacks: Shifts the problem to the customer and degrades the experience; it doesn't fix the information loss.
Vague instruction; the summary is still prone to paraphrasing or omitting exact numbers.
A larger window costs more on every turn and worsens "lost in the middle"; it doesn't specifically protect the critical facts.
Correct. Summaries lose exact values, IDs and dates; a case facts block preserves what cannot be paraphrased.

questoes.pergunta: NovaLar is defining when the agent should escalate to a human immediately. Which TWO triggers are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The model's self-reported confidence in the answer falls below 60%.
The customer explicitly asks to speak to a person.
The customer uses aggressive language or threatens to cancel the account.
The request requires an exception that the policy doesn't cover (e.g., a refund past the deadline for an unforeseen reason).
The conversation exceeds 20 turns.
questoes.explicacao: Escalate on an explicit request, a policy gap/exception or lack of progress; not on sentiment, self-reported confidence or conversation length.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern: self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; it doesn't work as a trigger.
Correct. An explicit request for a human is an immediate escalation trigger.
Anti-pattern of escalating based on sentiment; the agent can solve the underlying problem.
Correct. A policy gap or exception is outside the agent's autonomy; escalate.
Conversation length is not a criterion. What matters is lack of progress after reasonable attempts.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Vértice Software has about 40 developers and a monorepo with a C# (.NET) API and an Angular front end. The company is adopting Claude Code to generate and review code. Goals: have everyone follow the same conventions (naming, xUnit for tests, the dependency injection pattern) and speed up delivery. Constraints: no secrets may go into the repository, database migrations only go in with human review, and CI runs on GitHub Actions.

Today each developer pastes the team's conventions at the start of every session, and the results vary. Where should these conventions live?
opcoes: In CLAUDE.local.md at the root of the repository.
In each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, distributed by an onboarding script.
In the project's CLAUDE.md, versioned in the repository.
In a /conventions skill that each developer runs at the start of the session.
questoes.explicacao: Team conventions → project CLAUDE.md, versioned and loaded automatically.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored; it doesn't reach the other developers.
User scope is personal: each machine can diverge, and changes aren't versioned with the code.
Correct. The project CLAUDE.md is shared via git and loaded automatically for everyone working in the repo.
Depends on someone remembering to run it; permanent team conventions belong in CLAUDE.md, which loads on its own.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, a developer wants Claude Code to use the test database URL from her machine and to respond more concisely, without affecting her colleagues or versioning anything. Where should she put these instructions?
opcoes: In the project's CLAUDE.local.md.
In the project's CLAUDE.md, in a "Personal preferences" section.
In the project's .claude/settings.json.
In .claude/rules/personal.md with no frontmatter.
questoes.explicacao: Personal preferences for a project → CLAUDE.local.md (gitignored).
feedbacks: Correct. CLAUDE.local.md is for personal preferences specific to that project, without affecting the team.
It would affect everyone and would version data from her machine.
The project settings.json is shared and is meant for configuration (permissions, hooks), not for natural-language instructions.
Rules in .claude/rules/ are part of the versioned project; they would load for everyone.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice needs to migrate serialization from Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json. The change touches about 60 files, there are custom converters, and there are two possible approaches for handling polymorphic properties. How should the task be carried out in Claude Code?
opcoes: Request the migration file by file in separate sessions, with no overall plan.
Run with bypassPermissions so that the migration doesn't stop at any confirmation.
Use plan mode: explore, propose the approach, and only edit after approval.
Execute directly in acceptEdits mode to gain speed, reviewing the diff at the end.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode for a large, multi-file change with architectural decisions or several valid approaches.
feedbacks: Without a common approach, the result tends to be inconsistent across files (each session decides its own way).
bypassPermissions is not routine and doesn't address the need to decide on the approach before editing.
Correct. A multi-file change, with an architectural decision and more than one valid approach, is the typical plan mode case.
Skips the decision about the approach; with 60 files, fixing a wrong choice at the end is costly.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, which TWO tasks are suitable for direct execution, without plan mode? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Add a null check in OrderService.Calculate, pinpointed by a NullReferenceException stack trace.
Choose among three caching strategies for the product catalog and implement it.
Reorganize the project into vertical slices.
Change the value of a timeout constant in a single configuration file.
Switch the API's authentication from cookies to JWT, adjusting the API and the front end.
questoes.explicacao: Direct execution for small fixes with obvious scope; plan mode for multi-file changes or ones involving an architectural decision.
feedbacks: Correct. Localized fix, obvious scope and a clear instruction: direct execution.
There's a design decision between alternatives; plan and approve before editing.
Broad restructuring, with several valid approaches: a classic plan mode case.
Correct. A trivial, well-specified change.
Spans several modules and involves architectural decisions: it calls for plan mode.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice wants a /new-feature <name> command that generates the skeleton of a feature (controller, service, tests) following the team's pattern, available to everyone who clones the repo. What is the recommended approach?
opcoes: Create ~/.claude/skills/new-feature/SKILL.md on each developer's machine.
Create .claude/skills/new-feature/SKILL.md in the repo, receiving the name via $ARGUMENTS.
Package the command in a plugin published to an internal marketplace.
Describe the step-by-step in CLAUDE.md and ask the developer to type "create a new feature".
questoes.explicacao: Reusable team command → project skill in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (commands have been merged into skills).
feedbacks: Personal scope: it isn't shared through the repository, and each copy can diverge.
Correct. A versioned project skill is available to the team as /new-feature; $ARGUMENTS receives the parameter.
Possible, but more complex than necessary for a single command in a single repo.
Works poorly as a reusable command: it would bloat CLAUDE.md, which loads in every session, with an on-demand procedure.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice created the generate-migration skill, but Claude never uses it on its own when someone asks to "create the migration for the new column". The frontmatter has description: "Database utility". Which adjustment solves this?
opcoes: Rewrite the description to say what the skill does and when to use it (e.g., creating or altering EF Core migrations).
Add context: fork to the frontmatter, so that the skill runs in isolation and is chosen more easily.
Copy the skill's content into the project's CLAUDE.md, so that it's always in context when someone asks for migrations.
Add disable-model-invocation: true to the frontmatter, so that the model treats the skill as an explicit command.
questoes.explicacao: description/when_to_use determines when the skill is loaded automatically.
feedbacks: Correct. Automatic loading is driven by the description; a vague description doesn't match the user's request.
Defines where the skill runs (an isolated subagent), not when it's chosen.
Would load the procedure in every session, even when irrelevant; the problem is only the description.
Does the opposite: it prevents the model from invoking the skill on its own.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, the /audit-dependencies skill scans hundreds of .csproj and package.json files and dumps a lot of intermediate output into the conversation, polluting the main session's context. Which configuration solves this without changing what the skill does?
opcoes: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter, so that it runs in isolation.
Run /compact right after each execution of the skill.
Restrict the skill's allowed-tools to Read and Grep.
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/.
questoes.explicacao: Noisy, well-bounded work → isolate it in a subagent (context: fork) and return only the conclusion.
feedbacks: Correct. context: fork runs the skill in a separate context (CLAUDE.md loads, the history doesn't) and only the result comes back.
Remedies it after the fact, with loss of detail; the noise has already taken up the context and the summary may discard other useful things.
Limits the tools, but the intermediate output still lands in the main conversation.
Changes the availability scope, not the context isolation.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice's GitHub Actions job runs claude "review the changes in this PR" and hangs until it exceeds the runner's time limit. What is the most likely cause?
opcoes: -p (--print) is missing: without it, the session is interactive and waits for input.
The runner needs --dangerously-skip-permissions so that it doesn't stop at permission prompts.
--output-format json is missing; with text output, the runner doesn't detect the end of the process.
--max-turns is missing, so Claude entered an infinite tool loop.
questoes.explicacao: Claude Code in a pipeline requires -p/--print; without it, the process sits waiting for input.
feedbacks: Correct. In CI, -p is mandatory for non-interactive execution.
Skipping permissions is not the fix: without -p the process remains interactive. In CI, access is controlled with --allowedTools/--permission-mode.
The output format doesn't prevent termination; the problem is interactive mode.
--max-turns is a good backstop, but it doesn't explain hanging right at the start: the process is waiting for input.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, Claude wrote a date parser for reports, but it fails on time zones and on dates like Feb 29. After two rounds of "fix the edge cases", the errors keep showing up. Which refinement approach is the most effective?
opcoes: Repeat the request with more emphasis and detail: "handle ALL date edge cases, including time zones and leap years".
Ask Claude to list the edge cases it considers important and trust that list.
Write tests that fail on the edge cases, show the failures to Claude and iterate until they pass.
Ask Claude to rewrite the parser from scratch in a new session.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: failing tests + sharing the failures + iterating until they pass.
feedbacks: A vague instruction with no verifiable criterion; it's what has already failed twice.
Helps a little, but without executable tests there's no objective verification of the result.
Correct. TDD provides an objective definition of done and shows the model exactly where the error is.
Starts over with no new information about the failing cases; it will probably repeat the same mistakes.

questoes.pergunta: A Vértice developer resumed yesterday's session with --resume, but overnight a colleague merged a refactor that renamed folders and services. Claude keeps citing paths that no longer exist. What is the best way to proceed?
opcoes: Run /compact in the resumed session to clear out the old details.
Use --fork-session to create a branch of the old session and continue from it, without contaminating the original.
Start a new session with a structured summary of the decisions and the state of the task.
Continue the resumed session and correct Claude on every wrong path.
questoes.explicacao: Stale tool results → new session with a structured summary (or, at the very least, state explicitly what changed).
feedbacks: The summary may keep old paths as facts; it doesn't replace rereading the current code.
The fork inherits the same outdated history; it's meant for splitting paths off a common base, not for updating the base.
Correct. --resume is good when the tool results are still valid; if the code has changed a lot, start from scratch with a summary of what matters.
The history remains full of old reads; the model will keep tripping over them.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice requires that files in src/Infra/Migrations/ be changed only by humans, after review. Even with this rule in CLAUDE.md, Claude edited a migration while fixing a bug. How can the rule be guaranteed?
opcoes: Configure a PostToolUse hook that reverts any change in Migrations/ with git checkout.
Add src/Infra/Migrations/ to .gitignore and to claudeMdExcludes, to take the folder out of Claude's reach.
A PreToolUse hook (Edit/Write) in the project's .claude/settings.json that blocks paths in Migrations/ with exit 2.
Rewrite the rule prominently in CLAUDE.md and repeat it in a .claude/rules/ file with paths for Migrations/.
questoes.explicacao: A restriction that cannot fail → project PreToolUse hook blocking the tool (exit 2 / deny).
feedbacks: Acts after the edit and may undo legitimate work from other steps; the right thing is to prevent it beforehand.
Doesn't prevent the edit: .gitignore only affects versioning (and would break versioning of the migrations), and claudeMdExcludes only prevents loading CLAUDE.md files; it doesn't block tools.
Correct. A project hook is deterministic, applies to everyone and prevents the edit before it happens; the reason guides Claude.
It's still an instruction to the model, which is probabilistic; the rule is a compliance rule and needs a block in code.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, Claude Code is asked to find out where IPaymentGateway is implemented and how it's registered in dependency injection. It starts reading the project's files one by one, in alphabetical order. Which exploration strategy is correct?
opcoes: Grep for the interface name, read only the files found and follow the references with further Greps.
Read all of the project's .cs files first, to have the full context before answering.
Use Glob with **/*.cs, sort by size and read the 50 largest files, where business logic usually lives.
Ask the developer to provide the paths of the relevant files.
questoes.explicacao: Grep (content) → Read → follow references; don't read the entire codebase up front.
feedbacks: Correct. Incremental exploration: grep for the entry points, read, follow references. It saves context and gets straight to the point.
Anti-pattern of reading everything up front: it uses up context and degrades the quality of the answer.
Glob finds files by name/pattern, not by content; size doesn't indicate where the interface is.
The built-in tools handle this on their own; asking the human is unnecessary.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice wants to share a remote Jira MCP server with the whole team, but each developer has their own token. Which TWO practices are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Declare the server in the .mcp.json at the repo root with "type": "http" and the server's url.
Put a service account's token in .mcp.json, since the repository is private.
Reference the token in .mcp.json through an environment variable, for example "Authorization": "Bearer ${JIRA_TOKEN}".
Install it with the local scope, which saves to .claude/settings.local.json and is shared via git.
Omit the type field, because the presence of url already indicates that the server is HTTP.
questoes.explicacao: Shared MCP: .mcp.json (project scope) with an explicit type and secrets via ${VAR}.
feedbacks: Correct. .mcp.json is the project scope (shared via git), and a remote server needs a declared type.
A literal secret in a versioned file violates the secrets constraint and exposes the credential to everyone with access to the repo.
Correct. Secrets come in via ${VAR}; each developer sets their own value and nothing sensitive goes into git.
Double trap: the MCP local scope lives in ~/.claude.json, not in settings.local.json, and it isn't shared.
Trap: an entry with url and no type is read as stdio and fails.

questoes.pergunta: At Vértice, the same developer asks, in the same session in which Claude implemented a feature, "now review the code you wrote". The reviews almost never find problems, but bugs later show up in production. What explains this, and how should it be fixed?
opcoes: Reasoning-context bias: review in an independent session, not in the one that generated the code.
Lack of model capability: switch to a larger model just for the review step.
Review prompt too short: ask it to "be extremely critical and find at least 5 problems".
High temperature during generation: lower the temperature to generate more conservative code.
questoes.explicacao: An independent review (new session) avoids the bias of whoever generated the content.
feedbacks: Correct. A review in the same session inherits the generation's assumptions; a new session evaluates the code without that bias.
Doesn't address the cause: the problem is reviewing within the same context that generated the code.
Forces artificial findings (false positives) and keeps the context bias.
Doesn't explain the weak review; moreover, on newer models some sampling parameters aren't even accepted.

questoes.pergunta: Vértice automated PR review with the prompt "point out the important problems". 70% of the comments are about style (already covered by the linter), and the devs have started ignoring even the security alerts. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Add a second model that reviews and filters the first one's comments before posting them on the PR, discarding the irrelevant ones.
Ask the model for a confidence score for each comment and post only the comments scoring above 0.9.
Explicit criteria for what to report and what not to report (style already covered by the linter), with borderline examples.
Add "be conservative and avoid irrelevant comments".
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria (report / don't report / borderline) and turning off noisy categories preserve trust in the review.
feedbacks: More complex than necessary; without explicit criteria, the second model inherits the same ambiguity.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; it doesn't define what's relevant.
Correct. Explicit criteria reduce false positives; a noisy category erodes trust in the good ones, so you turn off the noisy one, refine it and turn it back on.
Vague instruction; it produces inconsistent results.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Instituto Áurea, a market analysis consultancy, is building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator receives the client's question and delegates to subagents for web search, document reading (PDFs and industry reports), data analysis and synthesis. The reports underpin investment decisions, so every claim needs a traceable source. Constraints: delivery within a few hours and controlled token cost.

To save time, an engineer proposes that the search subagent send its findings directly to the synthesis subagent, bypassing the coordinator. What is the best assessment?
opcoes: Reject it, because the Agent SDK doesn't allow a subagent to return data to another subagent.
Reject it: in hub-and-spoke, the coordinator routes all communication, handles errors and detects gaps.
Accept it, as long as the synthesis subagent has the Agent tool to request new searches from the search subagent when needed.
Accept it: direct communication reduces latency and tokens, and the coordinator can receive just the final report.
questoes.explicacao: Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator decomposes, delegates, routes all communication, aggregates and handles errors.
feedbacks: Wrong justification: the recommendation is architectural (observability and control), not a technical limitation.
Correct. Subagents talking directly to each other take away the coordinator's visibility to aggregate, handle failures and request a second round.
Creates a mesh of subagents calling subagents, which is harder to observe and control than hub-and-spoke.
Tempting because of the time savings, but it's an anti-pattern: the coordinator loses control over errors and coverage.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, the coordinator launches the analysis subagent with the prompt "Analyze the sources found and highlight the relevant numbers". The subagent returns generic text without citing any source at all. What is the most likely cause?
opcoes: The subagent's model is smaller than the coordinator's; using the same model would make the analysis cite the sources.
The subagent has an isolated context: the question, sources, criteria and format need to be explicit in the prompt.
A few-shot example of analysis with citations is missing from the coordinator's system prompt, which guides the subagents.
The subagent has too many tools and got lost choosing among searching, reading and analyzing, instead of using the sources.
questoes.explicacao: A subagent's context is isolated: everything it needs goes explicitly in the delegation prompt.
feedbacks: Switching the model doesn't give the subagent access to context that was never passed to it.
Correct. A subagent doesn't inherit the coordinator's conversation: "the sources found" don't exist for it.
The coordinator's system prompt doesn't reach the subagent; the problem is how context is passed.
Doesn't explain the absence of references; it simply didn't receive the sources.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, the coordinator delegates four independent searches (one per region). According to the logs, each subagent only starts when the previous one finishes, and the step takes four times longer than it should. How can it be parallelized?
opcoes: Give the search subagent all four regions in a single prompt, so that it does everything at once.
Have the coordinator emit the four Agent tool calls in the same response.
Increase the coordinator's max_tokens so that it can plan the four searches with more headroom.
Create four coordinators, one per region, each with its own search subagent.
questoes.explicacao: Subagent parallelism = multiple Agent calls in the same coordinator response.
feedbacks: Goes back to a single sequential flow and concentrates context in a single subagent.
Correct. Multiple Agent calls in the same turn run in parallel; separate turns are sequential.
Doesn't change the sequential execution; what parallelizes is emitting the calls in the same turn.
Multiplies the orchestration and complicates aggregation unnecessarily.

questoes.pergunta: Áurea received the request "Impact of generative AI on the creative industries". The final report came out well grounded, but it covers only visual arts and ignores music, film, games and advertising. The subagents did well what they were given. Where is the failure, and what is the fix?
opcoes: In the synthesis subagent: instruct it to generalize the visual arts conclusions to the other areas.
In the search subagent: instruct it to run broader searches and return more results.
In the coordinator's decomposition, which was too narrow: broaden it and check the coverage of the subareas.
In the model: switch the coordinator to a model with a larger context window.
questoes.explicacao: Decomposition too narrow → broaden it and check coverage explicitly in the coordinator.
feedbacks: Generalizing without evidence produces unsourced claims, which violates the traceability requirement.
Attacks the symptom in the wrong place: it searched for exactly what was delegated to it.
Correct. The subagents did what they were given; the gap originated in the decomposition. The fix is to broaden it and verify coverage.
The window isn't the problem; it was the decomposition that left out subareas.

questoes.pergunta: A client asks Áurea: "Why did our market share drop 8 points over the last year?". It isn't known in advance whether the cause is price, channel, a competitor or regulation. Which decomposition strategy is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Prompt chaining with fixed steps: collect data on price → channel → competition → regulation → synthesis.
A single large prompt asking the model to consider all possible causes at once.
Launch in parallel one subagent for every conceivable cause (20 subagents) and synthesize everything at the end.
Dynamic decomposition: the next subtasks emerge from what is discovered.
questoes.explicacao: Prompt chaining for known steps; dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation.
feedbacks: Chaining works when the steps are known in advance; here it spends equal effort on hypotheses that can be discarded and doesn't dig deeper into the one that gets confirmed.
Dilutes attention and doesn't allow digging deeper into whatever the first findings point to.
Expensive brute force, with no iterative refinement or focus.
Correct. Open-ended investigation: the subtasks emerge from the findings.

questoes.pergunta: Áurea is configuring the coordinator in the Agent SDK to delegate to subagents. Which TWO configurations are necessary or recommended? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Give every subagent the system's full set of tools, so that none of them gets stuck.
Include the Agent tool in the coordinator's allowedTools.
Skip the context in the delegation prompt, because subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's history.
Give the Agent tool to every subagent, so that they can call each other directly when needed.
Define each subagent (for example, with AgentDefinition) with a description, a prompt and a restricted set of tools.
questoes.explicacao: Coordinator with Agent in allowedTools; subagents defined with a description, a prompt and restricted tools.
feedbacks: Too many tools degrade selection; the ideal is 4 to 5 per agent.
Correct. Subagents are created by the Agent tool (formerly called Task); without it in allowedTools, the coordinator can't delegate.
False: a fresh subagent has an isolated context (what inherits the conversation is a fork, not a regular subagent).
Breaks hub-and-spoke: communication between subagents must go through the coordinator.
Correct. Specialized subagents, with a clear description and few tools, improve delegation and tool selection.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, even simple questions like "What was company X's net revenue in 2025?" go through all five subagents (search, documents, data, verification, synthesis) and cost as much as a full study. Which adjustment is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Have the coordinator invoke only the subagents that each query needs.
Keep the full pipeline to guarantee uniform quality, but use the Batch API to cut the cost in half.
Reduce each subagent's max_tokens to make simple questions cheaper.
Create a separate system, just for simple questions, with another coordinator.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator invokes only the subagents needed for the query.
feedbacks: Correct. A good coordinator chooses the subagents needed for each request, instead of always running the whole pipeline.
Batch isn't suited to interactive answers delivered within hours; and it still does unnecessary work.
Cuts output indiscriminately (including in complex studies) and doesn't avoid the useless calls.
Duplicates the architecture; the existing coordinator can decide the routing.

questoes.pergunta: Áurea's synthesis subagent has accumulated 18 tools (search, PDF reading, spreadsheets, charts, CRM, email...) and has started choosing the wrong tool frequently. The team has already improved the descriptions, but the problem persists. What is the recommended next step?
opcoes: Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing, for each tool, when to use it.
Force the order of use with tool_choice on every turn, according to a decision tree in the code.
Switch to a larger model, which handles many tools better.
Split it into specialized subagents, with 4 to 5 tools each.
questoes.explicacao: Too many tools in one agent → split into specialized subagents (4–5 tools each).
feedbacks: It's just another variation of "improve the descriptions", which already wasn't enough.
Hard-codes from the outside a decision tree that should belong to the model, and it's brittle.
May soften the symptom, but doesn't solve the excess of options at decision time.
Correct. With many tools, selection degrades even with good descriptions; the guideline is few tools per agent.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, the search_articles tool returns [] when the academic search API times out. The coordinator concluded in a report that "there is no literature on the topic". How should the tool behave?
opcoes: A structured error on timeout (transient, retryable); [] only when the search ran and found nothing.
Keep returning [], but with a note in the coordinator's system prompt saying that empty lists may mean an error.
Throw an exception that aborts the entire research pipeline.
Return {"error": "Search failed"}.
questoes.explicacao: Empty ≠ failure: structured error on timeout; empty list only when the search actually ran.
feedbacks: Correct. Empty is information ("nothing found"); a timeout means the search didn't run. Mixing the two leads to false conclusions.
Leaves the coordinator not knowing which case it is; the model will guess.
Aborting everything over a transient failure is disproportionate; the right thing is to propagate the structured error for a retry or an alternative.
Generic message: it doesn't say whether it's retryable, what was attempted or whether there's a partial result.

questoes.pergunta: Áurea's search subagent uses Anthropic's server-side web search and web fetch tools. Which TWO statements about these tools are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Web fetch works like a crawler: starting from a domain, it discovers and downloads the relevant pages.
You receive a web_search tool_use block, run the search on your server and return a tool_result.
They run at Anthropic and the result comes back in the same response; a tool error arrives with HTTP 200, inside the result.
pause_turn means that the search failed and the task should be aborted and reported as an error.
If the response comes back with stop_reason pause_turn, you should send it back so the model can continue the work.
questoes.explicacao: Server-side tools: they run at Anthropic, errors come with HTTP 200 inside the result, pause_turn → resend; web fetch only fetches URLs that are already present.
feedbacks: Web fetch only fetches URLs that are already present in the conversation; it's not a crawler.
That describes a client-side tool. Server-side tools are executed by Anthropic.
Correct. Server-side tools don't require you to execute anything, and the error comes inside the result, not as an HTTP failure.
pause_turn is not a failure; it's a pause in order to continue.
Correct. pause_turn indicates that the server-side loop hit its iteration cap; just resend to continue.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, each subagent returns its findings in free-form prose. In the synthesis, quotes end up associated with the wrong source and dates get lost. Which change best addresses the problem?
opcoes: Have the synthesis subagent research the source of each claim again before including it in the report.
Ask the subagents to always cite the sources in parentheses, right after each claim, with the full URL.
Structured output via JSON schema, separating the claim from the metadata (excerpt, source, publication date) in fields of their own.
Increase the subagents' max_tokens so that they describe the sources and dates in more detail in the text.
questoes.explicacao: Structured passing of findings (content separate from metadata) preserves provenance all the way to the synthesis.
feedbacks: Duplicates work and cost; the problem is how information is passed, not the search.
Helps little: the source is still mixed into the prose and gets lost or jumbled in the synthesis.
Correct. Separating the claim from the metadata preserves attribution through to the synthesis, without depending on parsing prose.
More text doesn't solve the lack of structure.

questoes.pergunta: Two reliable sources consulted by Áurea disagree on the size of the sodium battery market in the same year: US$ 4.2 bn (consultancy A) and US$ 5.1 bn (industry association B). How should the report handle the conflict?
opcoes: Use the average of the two (US$ 4.65 bn) as a consensus estimate between the sources.
Use the value from the source considered more authoritative and omit the other one.
Present both values with their sources and flag the figure as contested.
Omit the figure from the report due to the lack of consensus.
questoes.explicacao: Conflicting sources: record the diverging values with their sources; don't silently pick one or take an average.
feedbacks: Averaging invents a number that no source stated and hides the discrepancy.
Choosing silently hides the uncertainty from whoever is going to make the investment decision.
Correct. A conflict between sources should be made explicit, with each value's attribution, without silently picking one.
Loses relevant information; the right thing is to present it with the caveat.

questoes.pergunta: Áurea's verifier flagged as a "contradiction" that one source says 12,000 jobs in the sector and another says 15,000. On review, the first uses 2023 data and the second, 2025 data. What is the correct practice?
opcoes: Keep only the most recent number in the report and discard the 2023 one, since it's outdated.
Mark both values as contested and escalate the discrepancy to a human analyst to decide.
Average the two values to represent the period analyzed.
Record the data's reference date (in addition to publication and collection dates) and treat them as a time series, not a contradiction.
questoes.explicacao: Temporal data: record the reference date; values from different periods are not a contradiction.
feedbacks: Loses the historical series, which may be relevant, and doesn't teach the verifier to take dates into account.
Treats as a conflict something that isn't one; it creates unnecessary human work.
Invents a meaningless number.
Correct. Numbers from different periods don't contradict each other; temporal provenance avoids false alarms and makes it possible to show the trend.

questoes.pergunta: At Áurea, one of the six document-reading subagents failed because a PDF was corrupted, and the coordinator aborted the entire report. The client was left with nothing. What is the recommended behavior?
opcoes: Keep the abort, but notify the client with a generic error message.
Retry reading the PDF indefinitely until it works.
Omit the failed document from the report without mentioning it, since the other five documents are enough for the conclusion.
Proceed with the partial results, record the gap and offer alternatives (e.g., another version of the PDF).
questoes.explicacao: Error propagation: continue with the partial result, note the gap and offer an alternative.
feedbacks: Still wastes 5/6 of the work, and the generic message hides the diagnosis.
A corrupted file is not a transient failure; retrying doesn't solve it.
Silent suppression: the client doesn't know there's a gap and may make decisions on an incomplete basis.
Correct. A one-off failure shouldn't bring down the workflow: continue with the partial results, note the gap and offer an alternative.

questoes.pergunta: In long Áurea research tasks, the coordinator starts giving vague answers ("the typical trends in the sector") and forgets findings from hours earlier. Which TWO mitigations are the most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Place the key findings in the middle of the prompt, between the instructions and the documents.
Delegate high-volume exploration to subagents that return only summaries with the findings and the sources.
Persist findings and state in a scratchpad or manifest file that survives compression and allows resuming after failures.
Pass the coordinator the full text of every document read, taking advantage of the 1M-token window.
Increase the coordinator's max_tokens.
questoes.explicacao: Degraded context: subagents that summarize + state in a file/manifest; don't inflate the coordinator's context.
feedbacks: The middle is precisely the "lost in the middle" region; key findings go at the beginning.
Correct. The noise stays in the subagent's context; the coordinator receives only the essentials.
Correct. State kept in a file at a known location isn't lost in a summary or in a crash.
A large window isn't free: it increases the cost per turn and worsens "lost in the middle".
max_tokens limits the output; it doesn't help the model remember what went into the context.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Fluxa Contábil processes about 50,000 documents per month (invoices, receipts, contracts) for small businesses and extracts the fields into its clients' ERP. The pipeline, written in C#, calls the Messages API. Requirements: the output must follow a JSON schema, the totals must add up, and there is human review by sampling. Constraints: the backlog can be processed overnight, but uploads made through the app need a response within seconds.

Today the prompt says "respond only with the JSON" and about 3% of responses break the parser (trailing comma, a field with a different name, text before the JSON). What is the most robust fix?
opcoes: Structured outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) or a tool with input_schema and strict: true.
Post-process with a regex to extract the span between the first { and the last } and fix the commas.
Reinforce the prompt with "NEVER write anything outside the JSON" and an example of the expected format.
Prefill the assistant response with "{" to force the JSON to start.
questoes.explicacao: Guaranteed structured output: structured outputs (output_config.format) or a tool with input_schema + strict.
feedbacks: Correct. Structured output mechanisms guarantee schema conformance, something a text instruction doesn't guarantee.
A brittle patch: it doesn't fix fields with the wrong name or type.
Reduces the error rate, but remains probabilistic.
An old trick: it doesn't guarantee the schema and, on newer models, prefill returns 400.

questoes.pergunta: Many invoices processed by Fluxa don't include a due date. The current schema requires due_date as a mandatory string, and the model has been inventing plausible dates (issue date + 30 days). Which adjustment is correct?
opcoes: Keep the field required and add "don't invent dates" to the prompt.
Make due_date nullable and ask for null when the field doesn't exist.
Remove due_date from the schema.
Compute the date in code as issue date + 30 days when the model doesn't find the field.
questoes.explicacao: Data that may be missing → nullable field, so the model doesn't invent values.
feedbacks: The schema still requires a date; the instruction and the schema conflict, and the model tends to fill it in.
Correct. A nullable field gives the model a legitimate way out for missing data, instead of pressuring it to invent.
Loses the data in the documents that do include it.
Fabricates data the document doesn't contain, only in code; the ERP receives false information.

questoes.pergunta: At Fluxa, all responses already pass schema validation, but in 2% of invoices the total_amount field doesn't match the sum of the line items. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Resend the document asking it to "review your answer carefully", without detailing what's wrong.
Enable strict: true on the extraction tool, which guarantees that the extracted values are consistent with each other.
Overwrite total_amount in code with the sum of the items.
Validate the sum in code and, if it fails, send the specific errors back to the model, up to a limit of attempts.
questoes.explicacao: Semantic validation in code + retry with the specific errors in the prompt, up to a limit.
feedbacks: A retry without the specific errors wastes calls and tends to repeat the mistake.
strict guarantees format and types, not arithmetic or consistency between fields.
Hides the discrepancy: the declared total may be right and an item may have been extracted incorrectly.
Correct. Schema conformance doesn't guarantee semantic correctness; the validation loop with specific errors is the standard pattern.

questoes.pergunta: In Fluxa's validation loop, receipts without the issuer's CNPJ go into retry up to the 5-attempt limit, always failing on "issuer_cnpj required". The CNPJ really doesn't appear on these receipts. What should be done?
opcoes: Accept null when the data isn't in the source and route the document to human review.
Instruct the model to look up the CNPJ from the company's legal name in its training memory.
Increase the limit to 10 attempts.
Fill in "00.000.000/0000-00" to pass validation.
questoes.explicacao: Retries don't recover what isn't in the source: return null and handle the case.
feedbacks: Correct. Retries don't recover information that's missing from the source; the right thing is null and appropriate handling of the case.
Invites hallucination of tax data.
More attempts won't make the CNPJ appear in the document.
A fake value that passes the schema and pollutes the ERP; it hides the real absence.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa has a backlog of 200,000 old documents to process, as well as the app upload, which needs a response within seconds. Which TWO decisions are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Route the app upload through the Batch API too, polling the status every 10 seconds.
Match the batch results by submission order, since the API preserves order.
Implement the validation loop with retry inside a single batch request, across multiple turns.
Process the backlog through the Batch API, matching the results to the documents by custom_id.
Serve the app upload with synchronous calls to the Messages API.
questoes.explicacao: Batch for non-urgent volume (custom_id); synchronous for real time.
feedbacks: The Batch API has no SLA (it can take up to 24h); fast polling doesn't change that.
Trap: the results come back out of order; the link is the custom_id.
The Batch API doesn't support a multi-turn loop within a request; the retry becomes a new submission with the custom_ids that failed.
Correct. Non-urgent volume is the Batch API use case (50% cheaper, up to 24h); the results arrive out of order, hence the custom_id.
Correct. A real-time requirement rules out the Batch API, which has no SLA.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa has noticed that the model confuses "simple receipt" with "service invoice" in ambiguous documents and gets fields wrong on handwritten receipts. Which prompting technique is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Instruct: "be very careful with ambiguous and handwritten documents".
2 to 4 varied few-shot examples (one ambiguous, one handwritten), with the expected extraction and reasoning.
Add 20 examples of typed invoices, the most common type.
Ask the model for a per-field confidence score and automatically discard low-confidence extractions.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot: 2–4 varied examples with reasoning, focused on edge cases.
feedbacks: Vague instruction, with neither criteria nor a demonstration.
Correct. Targeted few-shot, with reasoning and covering edge cases, reduces classification errors and hallucination in extraction.
A volume of easy cases doesn't teach the boundary, which is where the errors are.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and doesn't improve extraction.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa's schema has expense_category as a free-form string, and the ERP receives variations such as "Food", "food", "Meals" and "Restaurant". Expenses outside the expected categories also show up. Which schema design is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Keep the free-form string and instruct the model to "always use the standardized names".
An enum with the ERP's categories plus "other", accompanied by a detail field for the unforeseen case.
Keep the free-form string and normalize it in the C# code with a synonym dictionary maintained by the team.
Use a strict enum with only the ERP's current categories, without any generic option.
questoes.explicacao: Enum + "other" with a detail field standardizes without forcing a wrong classification.
feedbacks: Without an enum, conformance relies on the prompt alone.
Correct. The enum standardizes the values; "other" + detail accommodates the unforeseen without forcing a wrong category.
Endless maintenance work; the schema can solve it at the source.
Forces the model to fit unforeseen expenses into a wrong category.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa's pipeline has fixed steps: classify the document type, extract with the type-specific schema and validate the totals. The steps don't change from one document to the next. Which architecture is the most appropriate?
opcoes: A single large prompt that classifies, extracts all possible schemas and validates, all at once.
An agentic loop with all tools available, letting the model decide the order of the steps.
Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of focused calls, with validation in code between stages.
A multi-agent coordinator with dynamic decomposition, which decides the stages for each document.
questoes.explicacao: Fixed, sequential steps → prompt chaining.
feedbacks: Dilutes attention and mixes responsibilities; makes it hard to validate and reprocess each stage.
Autonomy where there's no decision to make; less predictable and more expensive.
Correct. Sequential steps known in advance are the prompt chaining case, which is simple and predictable.
Unnecessary complexity for a fixed flow; dynamic decomposition is for open-ended investigation.

questoes.pergunta: On long contracts, Fluxa's extraction sometimes comes back with the JSON cut off in the middle. The C# code reads the content, tries to deserialize it, fails and logs "model returned invalid JSON". What should the code do first?
opcoes: Automatically resend the same request until a complete JSON comes back, with at most three attempts.
Check stop_reason before reading the content: max_tokens indicates truncated output, not invalid JSON.
Enable strict: true on the schema, which guarantees that the returned JSON is always complete.
Complete the truncated JSON in the code itself, closing any braces and brackets that were left open.
questoes.explicacao: Always check stop_reason: max_tokens means truncated output.
feedbacks: The same limit cuts it off again; it spends tokens without solving anything.
Correct. stop_reason tells you why generation stopped; max_tokens indicates truncation, not a formatting error.
strict doesn't prevent the cutoff caused by the output token limit.
Produces syntactically valid JSON, but with fields silently missing.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa defined the register_invoice tool with strict: true, but the API rejects the definition. In the input_schema, due_date and notes are not in required and there is no additionalProperties. What should be fixed?
opcoes: Declare additionalProperties: false; the two fields can remain optional, but the recommendation is to put them in required as nullable.
Add oneOf with two variations of the schema, one with a due date and one without, to cover both cases.
Remove strict: true, since the schema has optional fields.
Add additionalProperties: true to accept the optional fields.
questoes.explicacao: strict requires additionalProperties: false on every object; that's what is missing. Optional properties are allowed (they count toward a per-request limit [volatile]), but required + nullable makes the absence explicit.
feedbacks: Correct. The cause of the rejection is the missing additionalProperties: false. Optional fields are accepted by strict, but required + nullable is the recommended practice.
oneOf isn't among the constructs documented as supported, and it doesn't address the cause: additionalProperties: false is missing.
Gives up the schema guarantee based on a false premise: strict accepts optional fields.
It's the opposite of what strict requires.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa used tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "register_invoice"} to guarantee extraction. When migrating to a newer model, the requests started returning 400. The only purpose of forcing it was to get the JSON. What is the recommended fix?
opcoes: Go back to the previous model permanently.
Prefill the assistant with the beginning of a tool_use block.
Switch to tool_choice any, which is accepted on all models.
Migrate to structured outputs (output_config.format).
questoes.explicacao: Forcing a tool just to get JSON → structured outputs on newer models (support is per model: check the capabilities).
feedbacks: Works around it without solving it and locks the pipeline out of upgrades.
Prefill returns 400 on newer models.
any is also rejected on newer models and, in any case, doesn't guarantee which tool would be called.
Correct. On newer models, forced tool_choice (any/tool) returns 400; structured outputs is the direct path to JSON that follows the schema.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa wants a GitHub Actions job that, on every PR that changes extraction schemas, uses Claude Code to run the extraction on a set of sample documents and blocks the merge if anything regresses. The result needs to be read by a script. Which configuration is the most appropriate?
opcoes: claude -p with --resume of yesterday's session, reusing the context of the documents already analyzed.
claude -p with --output-format text and a grep for "APPROVED" in the output.
Submit the documents through the Batch API and check the result the next day.
claude -p with --output-format json, --json-schema, --max-turns and restricted --allowedTools.
questoes.explicacao: CI: -p + --output-format json + --json-schema, with --max-turns and --allowedTools.
feedbacks: Reuses possibly outdated results; each CI run should be independent and reproducible.
Parsing free text is brittle; the CLI offers JSON output with a schema.
Batch isn't suited to a blocking pre-merge check: it has no SLA.
Correct. -p for non-interactive execution, schema-validated JSON output for the script, and turn and tool limits as a backstop.

questoes.pergunta: A Fluxa developer is going to use Claude Code to implement support for a new document type (bill of lading), but the requirements are unclear: nobody knows which fields the ERP needs or how to handle multi-page documents. Which approach is the most appropriate to start with?
opcoes: Use bypassPermissions so that Claude explores and implements everything without interruptions.
Ask Claude to choose the most common fields in transport documents and proceed with the implementation.
Ask for the implementation directly and adjust later, as errors show up.
Ask Claude to interview the developer about fields, formats and edge cases before implementing.
questoes.explicacao: Unclear requirements → interview (Claude asks questions before implementing), possibly followed by plan mode.
feedbacks: Doesn't solve the lack of requirements and removes safety controls.
Decides by assumption something that needs to come from the business (what the ERP expects).
Creates rework: wrong decisions about fields and pagination contaminate the code.
Correct. With unclear requirements, the interview technique surfaces the decisions before any code is written.

questoes.pergunta: At Fluxa, schema files are scattered across src/*/Schemas/*.json, in several projects, and all of them must follow the same convention (snake_case, optional fields as nullable, a description on every property). How should this convention be passed to Claude Code?
opcoes: Put the convention in the root CLAUDE.md.
A rule in .claude/rules/ with paths: "src/**/Schemas/*.json".
Create a CLAUDE.md in each Schemas/ folder with the same convention.
Create a /schema skill that the developer invokes when editing schemas.
questoes.explicacao: Convention for a file type scattered across the repo → .claude/rules/ with paths (glob).
feedbacks: It works, but it loads in every session even when nobody is touching schemas; a path-scoped rule is more precise.
Correct. A convention that cuts across directories calls for a rule with a path glob: it covers future folders and doesn't duplicate content.
Duplication that diverges over time and doesn't automatically cover new folders.
Depends on someone remembering to invoke it; the path-scoped rule loads on its own.

questoes.pergunta: Fluxa reports 97% aggregate accuracy and reviews a uniform 5% sample of documents. Even so, clients complain about frequent errors on handwritten receipts. Which TWO actions are the most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Break down accuracy by document type and by field, to find where the failures are concentrated.
Process each handwritten receipt three times and keep the most frequent result.
Use the model's self-reported confidence to decide what to review, without calibrating it on a labeled set.
Increase the uniform sample from 5% to 10%.
Replace uniform sampling with risk-stratified sampling, reviewing high-risk types proportionally more.
questoes.explicacao: Break the metric down by type and field; review with risk-stratified sampling.
feedbacks: Correct. The aggregate metric hides per-segment failures: 97% overall can coexist with poor performance on handwritten documents.
Triples the cost without measuring or fixing the cause.
Uncalibrated confidence means nothing.
Doubles the cost without directing the review to where the errors are.
Correct. Human review should concentrate where the risk is highest.
